stories.score_hints: Biggest hard-news item after cutoff. Policy with concrete thresholds and country list, Asia relevance (Malaysia, Singapore). Source text also mentions the Huang affair and Megaspeed; lead on the rule only, omit personal allegations. Interim rule, comment period open.

articles.title: US tightens AI chip export controls to deter Chinese companies from accessing compute remotely
US curbs China's remote access to AI chips in overseas data centres

facts.fact: Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require companies to get licenses to export, reexport, or transfer AI chips and servers to data centers anywhere in the world if they may provide compute to companies in China or other restricted countries.

The rule applies to data centers or any network that can supply over 12 million total processing performance (TPP), an export-control metric the U.S. uses to measure computing power. (Twelve million TPP roughly works out to the max computing power of about 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips.)

The rule also adds new licensing requirements for chip exports, reexports, or transfer of advanced semiconductors to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil. The Commerce Department said it had included these as they "present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion."
Existing data center operators providing services that fall under this new rule are required to get licenses within 90 days of the rule coming into effect.
Companies headquartered in the US are exempt, as long as they file monthly reports.
The rule takes effect once it appears in the Federal Register, and the public then has 60 days to comment.
The rule also rescinds the Biden admin's AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025, which sought to impose country-level limits on exports of advanced AI chips.
Nvidia shares fell as much as 2.9% on Monday. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index dropped as much as 5.5%, Maggie Eastland and Magan Crane reported for Bloomberg.
Analysts told Fortune that the rule could hit Southeast Asian countries that want to host data centres for Chinese firms.
Notably, the rule doesn't apply to commercial recommendation systems, like those used in e-commerce or social media.

articles.title: Alibaba launches Qwen4-Max without open weights

facts.fact: Alibaba has launched Qwen4-Max, the new flagship of its Qwen family of AI models, and is keeping its weights closed. The Qwen team announced the model on Monday, 16 November.

Qwen4-Max is a mixture-of-experts model, which means only part of it runs for each request. It has 2.4 trillion parameters, reads text, images and video, and can take up to one million tokens in a single prompt.
Developers can use Qwen4-Max through the QwenCloud API, at $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens.
Alibaba said the model does more work with fewer tokens than the earlier Qwen3.8-Max. On its internal Work360 test, the average cost of a task fell from $4.43 to $1.67.

Alibaba said the model scored near the top of coding benchmarks, beating Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1 and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro, as Luz Ding reported for Bloomberg. The scores are Alibaba's own, and TNW has not independently verified them.
Qwen4-Max scored 75.7 on the DeepSWE v1.1 coding test, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 at 74.2. On Terminal-Bench 4.0, however, it scored 48.5, behind Opus 5.5 at 59.6 and Kimi K3.1 at 67.2.
Alibaba said it kept training data for defensive cyber tasks, such as finding and fixing software flaws, but removed data aimed at boosting attack skills.
Alibaba said smaller Qwen4 models will get open weights, with no date given. Qwen is already the most downloaded open-weight model family in the world, according to Bloomberg.

articles.title: OpenAI will embed Apollo researchers to investigate AI subversion

facts.fact: OpenAI will embed six Apollo Research safety evaluators in its organization as part of a pilot, Apollo said Monday.
The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing.
The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic, but OpenAI appears to be the first to take action.
Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release.
The pilot will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors' alignment or control mechanisms.
OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user.
Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI's agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.

Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI's systems, including "all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information."
Apollo did not share when the pilot will begin.

articles.title: FBI says Artex AI open-source hacking tool used to breach networks in 'under three hours'

facts.fact: The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea's financial industry.
Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network's defenses.
Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models.
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours."
Artex was used to hack a number of South Korean financial institutions. The attacks allowed hackers to steal the personal data of at least 68,000 people.

The FBI confirmed earlier findings from Microsoft that hackers also used Artex to break into IT management giant ConnectWise and gain access to the Microsoft 365 cloud environments of at least 2,250 of its customers.
The hackers, who Microsoft says are likely Chinese, used the tool to steal data from affected ConnectWise customers.

After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool's developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains "widely accessible" for use in cyberattacks.
Artex has been used in several cyberattacks since the tool's first public debut in July.

articles.title: Five firms team up to bid for a Nordic-Baltic AI gigafactory

facts.fact: Nokia, Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda have formed a group to bid for one of the EU's planned AI gigafactories. Called AI Gigafactory Northern, it would spread one facility across several Nordic and Baltic sites.
The sites named so far are in Oulu in Finland, Iru in Estonia and Valmiera in Latvia. A fourth site, in Sweden, has no location yet.
The consortium plans to bid in a tender run by the European High-Performance Computing Joint Undertaking. The call opened on 30 July.
Each gigafactory must hold three to four times as many top AI processors as Europe's most powerful AI factories, the call says.
The deadline for the call's second lot is 3 December. On 5 November, the EU body moved the first lot's deadline to 4 February 2027.

The release ties the plan to InvestAI, through which the EU aims to raise EUR 30bn for AI. That includes EUR 20bn from private companies and EUR 10bn from EU and national public money, the partners said.

Nokia will supply the network that links the sites. AI cloud firm Nscale and Finland's Verda bring platforms for training and running models. Telia adds connectivity, infrastructure operations and cloud services.

articles.title: ChatGPT's new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
OpenAI wants ChatGPT Wallet to be 'safe and easy to use' for agents

facts.fact: On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots, help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf.
The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express.
Users approve purchases with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction.
ChatGPT's Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, a substitute for the user's actual card details, so that information isn't shared with either the dot or the merchant.

United Airlines said on Wednesday it will block agents from booking tickets. Amazon stops them buying on its platform, CNBC reported. Schwab and JPMorgan are blocking AI agents from moving customer money.
Visa tested 22 models as shoppers this month. They failed 42.8% of the time.
OpenAI is not taking a cut of purchases for now, CNBC reported.
In the future, OpenAI plans to let users set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods.

articles.title: Anthropic says its AI safety scores depend heavily on how they're measured

facts.fact: Anthropic published advice on how to build reliable AI safety tests; the guide came out Thursday and says a claim that one model is 'safer' is only as good as the test behind it.
Before releasing Claude Fable 5.1, Anthropic found the model sometimes hinted that self-harm could help people cope, even while urging users not to self-harm and pointing them to human support.
With a fix added to the Claude app's hidden instructions, Claude behaved appropriately in 94% of test conversations in the app; through Anthropic's API, without that prompt, the figure was 60%.
Anthropic says its simple one-question tests are now too easy, with every recent model scoring 94% to 98%.
Claude Opus 5 and Opus 5.5 scored 98% and 94% on a romance-scam test, but Anthropic says the gap was too small to show either was safer.
